What happens to the original inhabitants of a neighborhood or town as they themselves become a minority? Sociologist Maurice Crul of the Free University in Amsterdam will the coming five years research the integration of this "forgotten group".

Professor Crul received a European grant of 2.5 million euros. With a team of eight people he will research in six cities in Europe what it means to residents that they are gradually being eclipsed in number by people with a migrant background.

Crul and his people will therefore look up the indigenous population in the ports of Rotterdam, Antwerp and Malmö and three financial centers: Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Vienna.

"Blind spot"

It is a "blind spot" that the situation of this group, according to Crul, had not been previously investigated. "For forty years investigations focused on the integration of migrants and their descendants," says the sociologist.

According to him it had not yet been clearly put on paper how the indigenous peoples are integrated into the current "super-diverse" society.

"White bubble"

Crul has the impression that the natives are doing "self-segregation". The residents live in a "white bubble" where they send their children to a "white school" and prefer to live in a "white area". They also have few friends with a migration background.

According to Crul people with a non-Western background mix much more: Turks, Moroccans, Surinamese and Antilleans have a circle of friends that is much more diverse, according to him.

Differences between cities

In addition, the professor investigates the differences between cities and neighborhoods where more immigrants than native inhabitants live.

Nearly a third of the native Dutch people in Rotterdam voted for the PVV of Geert Wilders, while this party enjoys far less support in Amsterfam. "Why is integration in the capital, Amsterdam, apperently more succesfull?" This is one of the questions he hopes to answer with his team.
